title: Strava's heatmap outlined military bases
hook: Soldiers' jogging routes, combined into an 'anonymous' map, drew the outlines of secret sites.
collected: GPS traces from about a billion recorded activities.
howObtained: Users recorded runs and rides with Strava and fitness devices.
inferred: Where people repeatedly exercise, which reveals the shape of bases and patrol routes.
done: Strava published an aggregated global heatmap. Analyst Nathan Ruser pointed out it revealed military bases and routes, including in conflict zones.
affected: Military personnel and anyone in sparse areas.
label: DOCUMENTED
labelNote: The heatmap was public; the revealed sites were independently confirmed by journalists.

companyResponse.text: "We are committed to helping people better understand our settings to give them control over what they share."
companyResponse.source: Strava, to the Washington Post via TechCrunch

outcome.text: The US military reviewed its use of personal devices and apps.

sources.title: US military reviewing tech use after Strava privacy snafu

limits: No individual was named. The harm came from the pattern.
whyItMatters: Aggregate, 'anonymous' data can still reveal secrets about places and groups.

title: The Netflix Prize data was de-anonymised
hook: A handful of movie ratings and dates could pick out a subscriber.
collected: Movie ratings and dates from about 500,000 Netflix subscribers, released 'anonymised' for a contest.
inferred: Identity, by matching to public IMDb reviews.
done: Narayanan and Shmatikov (IEEE S&P 2008) showed that a few ratings with approximate dates are enough to make most records unique, and matched some records to public IMDb profiles.
label: DOCUMENTED
labelNote: Peer-reviewed research. The famous high percentages describe how UNIQUE records are, not how many people were actually named; the real IMDb test was small.

outcome.text: Netflix cancelled a planned second contest after a lawsuit and regulator questions.

sources.title: Robust De-anonymization of Large Sparse Datasets

limits: Uniqueness is not the same as identification.
whyItMatters: 'Anonymous' is often a promise that can't be kept.

title: "Unique in the Crowd": four location points
hook: Four places and times were enough to single out 95% of 1.5 million phone users.
collected: 15 months of phone-antenna location records for 1.5 million people.
howObtained: Mobile operator data provided to researchers.
inferred: Whether a person's trace is unique.
done: de Montjoye et al. (Scientific Reports, 2013) found that 4 hourly, antenna-level points uniquely identify 95% of individuals in the dataset.
label: DOCUMENTED
labelNote: Peer-reviewed. 'Unique' is not the same as 'named'. Naming someone needs outside information.

sources.title: Unique in the Crowd: The privacy bounds of human mobility

limits: Antenna-level data; GPS would be more precise still.
whyItMatters: Your movements are like a signature.

title: 15 demographic facts could re-identify 99.98% of Americans (model estimate)
hook: Age, ZIP, gender and a few more details go a long way.
inferred: Likelihood that a record is correctly re-identified.
done: Rocher, Hendrickx and de Montjoye (Nature Communications, 2019) estimated that 15 demographic attributes would correctly re-identify 99.98% of Americans in any dataset.
label: DOCUMENTED
labelNote: Peer-reviewed. This is a model ESTIMATE, not a count of real re-identifications.

sources.title: Estimating the success of re-identifications in incomplete datasets using generative models

whyItMatters: Removing names does not make data anonymous.

title: Motion sensors can leak what you tap
hook: Researchers inferred PINs from the tiny tilts of a phone, using JavaScript in a web page.
howObtained: Apps (TouchLogger, 2011) and web pages (TouchSignatures, 2016) reading motion sensors.
inferred: Taps, scrolls, and digits typed on a keypad.
done: Cai and Chen (2011) inferred over 70% of keys on a number pad from orientation data in an Android app. Mehrnezhad et al. (2016) showed JavaScript could distinguish touch actions and infer PINs; browser makers adopted countermeasures.
label: DOCUMENTED
labelNote: Peer-reviewed research under lab conditions. No evidence of widespread real-world abuse.

companyResponse.text: Mozilla, Google, Apple and Opera adopted some countermeasures, according to the researchers; iPhones now require permission for motion data in web pages.

sources.title: TouchSignatures: Identification of User Touch Actions and PINs Based on Mobile Sensor Data via JavaScript

whyItMatters: Capability is not proof of use, but it explains why permissions exist.
